note: `commitwork scan` runs EVERY check in checks[] (groups are only for `run <group>`). So a sweep runs all scanners, static + deep + runtime. Runtime scanners (requiresUrl) skip visibly as a coverage void when no live URL is supplied — never silently absent.

checks.description: Verified/unknown secrets across git history (TruffleHog)
checks.remediationPrompt: You are fixing secrets that TruffleHog found in this repo's git HISTORY (not just the working tree). Read trufflehog.json — each result has DetectorName, the file/commit, and a Verified flag. For every VERIFIED secret: (1) rotate/revoke the credential at its provider immediately — a secret in git history is already compromised, removing it from source is not enough; (2) remove the value from current source and move it to an env var / secret manager; (3) note that scrubbing it from history (git filter-repo / BFG) requires a force-push and team coordination — propose it, do not run it. For UNVERIFIED results, confirm whether each is a real credential or a false positive before acting. Never print the raw secret values in your response. Show the source diff and the rotation checklist.
local: SFX=$(node "$CW_ROOT/bin/scan-config-suffix.mjs" 2>/dev/null || true); set --; [ -n "$SFX" ] && set -- --exclude-paths "$CW_ROOT/manifests/trufflehog-exclude.self.txt"; trufflehog git file://. $([ "${CW_DEPTH_RANK:-2}" -lt 2 ] && echo --max-depth=1000) --json --no-update --results=verified,unknown "$@" > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/trufflehog.json" 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/trufflehog.log"; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/trufflehog.json.exit"
checks.formatNotes: TruffleHog outputs JSON-lines (one object per line), not a single array. An empty findings file is NOT on its own a clean report: it is also what a run killed on its first syscall leaves. Every run ends with a structured receipt on stderr — captured to trufflehog.log — of the form {"msg":"finished scanning","chunks":N,"bytes":N,"verified_secrets":N,...}. parseReport REQUIRES that receipt before scoring an empty report clean, reports chunks/bytes in the summary so the claim can be checked, and treats chunks:0 (finished, examined nothing) and an absent receipt as noscan. The runner also records the process exit code to trufflehog.json.exit; it is consulted only once the parse has already concluded 'nothing found', because a non-zero exit is the normal successful state for many scanners. Verified against trufflehog 3.97.0 on 2026-08-22 — re-verified after 3.95.9/3.96.0 were found to emit a mass FALSE VERIFIED on the Lob detector (1,311 of 1,314 published criticals fleet-wide; 207 on one repo at 3.96.0, 0 on the same repo at 3.97.0). The lesson is the reason the version now travels with the finding: a verified:true from this tool is only as good as the build that produced it. EGRESS: verifiers. `--results=verified,unknown` sends every candidate to the issuing service (AWS STS, GitHub, Slack, …) to ask whether it is live; `--no-update` only stops the self-update. Under the host sandbox the filesystem is confined and the network is open (isolation fs-only).

checks.description: Fast filesystem secret scan (Gitleaks) — complements the TruffleHog git-history pass and gives a pre-commit hook. SCOPE IS BOUNDED by manifests/gitleaks.toml: dependency trees, build output and runtime data are skipped, so a scan that reports clean has not looked everywhere. The bound is not a silent cap — the scope file states every exclusion and why.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are fixing leaked secrets found by gitleaks in this repo. For each finding in gitleaks.json (each has RuleID, File, StartLine, and a redacted Secret): rotate the secret at its provider, remove it from source, move it to an env var / secret store (and reference it via config, e.g. process.env / Spring @Value / a mounted secret), and add a .gitleaksignore entry ONLY for confirmed false positives (test fixtures, example keys, public identifiers) with a one-line reason. Do not silence a real secret with an ignore. Show the diff for every file you touch.
local: SFX=$(node "$CW_ROOT/bin/scan-config-suffix.mjs" 2>/dev/null || true); gitleaks detect --no-git --source . --config "$CW_ROOT/manifests/gitleaks${SFX}.toml" --max-target-megabytes 50 --report-format json --report-path "$CW_REPORT_DIR/gitleaks.json" --redact >"$CW_REPORT_DIR/gitleaks.log" 2>&1; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/gitleaks.json.exit"
checks.formatNotes: FORMAT FACTS (do not improvise): a .gitleaksignore file is PLAIN LINES, one fingerprint per line, # for comments. Each finding's Fingerprint field in gitleaks.json IS the exact line to use, verbatim — for this repo's --no-git scan it has the shape file:rule:line. Column ranges are never part of a fingerprint, and TOML [allowlist] sections belong to gitleaks.toml, NOT .gitleaksignore. gitleaks-verify.json carries a three-state verdict per finding (verified/refuted/unknown) produced by monitor/secret-verify.mjs; it holds verdicts and provenance only, never a secret. Its ABSENCE means every row is undetermined, which is not the same as safe. EGRESS: verifiers. gitleaks itself makes no network call; the second command, monitor/secret-verify.mjs, feeds its candidates to the TruffleHog verifiers, which contact the issuing services. Under the host sandbox the filesystem is confined and the network is open (isolation fs-only).

checks.description: Filesystem secret scan with Betterleaks, the gitleaks successor, as a second engine over the same scope file (manifests/gitleaks.toml). It adds rules gitleaks lacks (generic-password, generic-credential-uri, azure-storage-account-key), a per-finding confidence, and inline validation against the issuing services. Overlaps secrets-gitleaks by design, so its counts stay out of the headline total.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are fixing leaked secrets found by betterleaks in this repo. For each finding in betterleaks.json (RuleID, File, StartLine, a redacted Secret, Attributes.confidence, and ValidationStatus when a validator exists): treat ValidationStatus 'valid' as a live credential and rotate it at its provider before touching code; remove every real secret from source and read it from an env var or secret store instead. A low-confidence generic-* finding is a candidate, not a verdict: read the line before acting, and add a .gitleaksignore entry ONLY for confirmed false positives (test fixtures, example keys, public identifiers) with a one-line reason. Do not silence a real secret with an ignore. Show the diff for every file you touch.
local: SFX=$(node "$CW_ROOT/bin/scan-config-suffix.mjs" 2>/dev/null || true); CFG=gitleaks; [ -n "$SFX" ] && CFG=betterleaks.self; betterleaks dir . --config "$CW_ROOT/manifests/$CFG.toml" --max-target-megabytes 50 --report-format json --report-path "$CW_REPORT_DIR/betterleaks.json" --redact --no-banner --no-color --exit-code 0 --regex-engine stdlib --validation --validation-timeout 10s >"$CW_REPORT_DIR/betterleaks.log" 2>&1; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/betterleaks.json.exit"
checks.formatNotes: FORMAT FACTS (do not improvise): betterleaks.json is gitleaks' JSON array, so .gitleaksignore applies unchanged and each Fingerprint is the exact line to use. Two fields are added. Attributes.confidence is low, medium or high; low marks a generic-* pattern match and is a triage signal, never a severity. ValidationStatus is valid, invalid, revoked, error or unknown, and is ABSENT for a rule with no validator; absence means not checked, which is not the same as safe. --exit-code 0 makes betterleaks.json.exit mean the tool ran, not that it found nothing. --regex-engine stdlib is Go's own RE2-semantics engine. The default re2 engine runs a WebAssembly build that caches itself under ~/Library/Caches/com.github.wasilibs; the host sandbox denies that write and betterleaks 1.9.0 panics on it, and both engines found the same 87 fingerprints on this repository (2026-10-07). betterleaks.log carries the 'scanned ~N bytes' receipt and a 'validation complete' line with per-status counts. EGRESS: verifiers. --validation sends each candidate to its issuing service to test it, the same egress the gitleaks lane's verify pass has. Under the host sandbox the filesystem is confined and the network is open (isolation fs-only).

checks.description: Static analysis with Semgrep auto rules (SARIF)
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging and fixing SAST findings from Semgrep (semgrep.sarif, SARIF format). For each result: read runs[].results[] — ruleId, message.text, and the file+region in locations[].physicalLocation. Work highest severity first (security-severity property, else level=error). For each real finding, fix the ROOT CAUSE, not the symptom: parameterize SQL instead of concatenating, encode/escape output at the sink for XSS, replace weak crypto/hashing, remove hardcoded credentials, validate/allowlist user-controlled paths and commands. For a genuine false positive, add a `// nosemgrep: <ruleId>` comment with a one-line justification rather than deleting the rule. Do not suppress a finding you have not understood. Show a diff per fix and note any that need a human decision.
local: semgrep scan --config p/default $([ "${CW_DEPTH_RANK:-3}" -ge 2 ] && echo --config p/owasp-top-ten) $([ "${CW_DEPTH_RANK:-3}" -ge 3 ] && echo --config p/security-audit) --config "$CW_ROOT/manifests/semgrep-taint" ${CW_SEMGREP_PRO:+--pro-intrafile} --metrics=off --sarif --output "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep.sarif" --exclude reference --exclude reports --quiet . 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep.log"; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep.sarif.exit"

if [ -n "$CW_SEMGREP_PRO" ]; then semgrep scan --config p/default $([ "${CW_DEPTH_RANK:-3}" -ge 2 ] && echo --config p/owasp-top-ten) $([ "${CW_DEPTH_RANK:-3}" -ge 3 ] && echo --config p/security-audit) --config "$CW_ROOT/manifests/semgrep-taint" --metrics=off --sarif --output "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep-oss.sarif" --exclude reference --exclude reports --quiet . 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep-oss.log"; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep-oss.sarif.exit"; fi
checks.formatNotes: Semgrep may 404 a ruleset URL and load ZERO rules, then exit 7. The manifest catches exit 7 with `|| true`, so only the report survives. An empty results[] with no toolExecutionNotifications is genuinely clean; a non-empty toolExecutionNotifications with empty results[] indicates failure. parseReport checks both channels.
checks.notes: The local taint pack was added 2026-08-25 after measuring that the three registry packs produced BYTE-IDENTICAL output with and without --pro-intrafile: same 368 rules, same finding, same rule id. The Pro engine was engaging and had nothing to do. manifests/semgrep-taint/ gives it work from rules we control and can enumerate, and monitor/test/semgrep-taint.test.mjs enforces the entry condition that every rule there must find something the OSS engine cannot — so the account dependency is load-bearing rather than decorative. FROM 2026-08-29 THE ENGINE IS ALLOCATED PER REPOSITORY: Pro is licensed for a bounded number of repos (monitor/registry.mjs SEMGREP_PRO_MAX) and this fleet resolves to 119, so the flag is conditional on $CW_SEMGREP_PRO, which monitor/sweep.mjs sets per repo from the registry's semgrepPro.repos. A repo outside the allocation runs the OSS engine and its findings are REAL — the narrower engine is a coverage bound (scan-scope's engine-per-repo note), not a discount on the number. The taint pack above therefore contributes nothing on an OSS repo by design, which is the coverage bound doing its job rather than a lane failing. Which engine actually ran is recorded by the run itself at runs[].tool.driver.name ('Semgrep PRO' / 'Semgrep OSS'), so the allocation is checkable against the artifact instead of believed from this manifest.

checks.description: SAST via Opengrep — the OSS fork of Semgrep, AT MEASURED PARITY WITH IT AND 4.6x FASTER. Not a standby; the word was wrong and is retired here. Measured 2026-08-11 against opengrep 1.26.0: it consumes the same rule YAML, resolves the same `p/` registry packs, emits the same SARIF including invocations[], and fails closed on a 404'd ruleset exactly as Semgrep does — so parseReport's tool-failure guard already covers it with no new format. MEASURED AGAIN 2026-08-26, 5 repos of the 100RandomRepos corpus (cheerio, undici, reflex, revive, grpc-java), identical packs, semgrep 1.172.0 without --pro-intrafile so the engine is the only variable: RESTRICTED TO THE RULES BOTH ENGINES LOADED, semgrep 346 findings and opengrep 347 — exact parity plus one, opengrep finding a reflex row semgrep missed. Wall clock 806s vs 176s, and 125s vs 16s on undici. The raw totals (394 vs 347) differ by ONE RULE, java.lang.security.audit.active-debug-code-printstacktrace at 48 hits, which is not in opengrep's loaded set at all: from the same `p/` names semgrep resolved 3033 rules and opengrep 1157. THAT IS REGISTRY RULE RESOLUTION, NOT ENGINE CAPABILITY, and pinning both engines to a vendored rule set closes it. DO NOT PASS `--pro`: measured 2026-08-26, it prints a full scan banner, exits 0, and writes a SARIF with 0 results and 0 rules where the same command without it yields 175 — a silent clean, the exact class the reporting checks must detect. `--dataflow-traces` runs but emits no codeFlows, and there is no working interfile mode behind the inherited Pro flags. NOT IN THE `all` GROUP because it runs the same rules over the same tree as `sast`, so scheduling both would report every finding twice — that is an argument for choosing ONE engine, never a reason to ship one that runs nowhere. It sits in `compare` beside sast-auto so a named group reaches it; swapping it into `all` in place of `sast` is an operator re-basis, not a side effect. [RESTORED 2026-09-02 by session 4e7722b2 from a transcription in evaluations/RECOVERY-opengrep-manifest-2026-09-01.md, after this field was lost from the working tree. Transcribed from a diff, not from the original file — re-derive from your own scrollback if you have it.]
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging and fixing SAST findings from Opengrep (opengrep.sarif, SARIF format). Opengrep is the OSS fork of Semgrep and its findings are the same shape: read runs[].results[] — ruleId, message.text, and the file+region in locations[].physicalLocation. Work highest severity first (security-severity property, else level=error). For each real finding, fix the ROOT CAUSE, not the symptom: parameterize SQL instead of concatenating, encode/escape output at the sink for XSS, replace weak crypto/hashing, remove hardcoded credentials, validate/allowlist user-controlled paths and commands. For a genuine false positive, add a `// nosemgrep: <ruleId>` comment — Opengrep honours the same directive — with a one-line justification rather than deleting the rule. Do not suppress a finding you have not understood. Show a diff per fix and note any that need a human decision.
local: opengrep scan --config p/default --config p/owasp-top-ten --config p/security-audit --sarif --output "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep.sarif" --exclude reference --exclude reports --quiet . 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/opengrep.log"; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/semgrep.sarif.exit"
checks.formatNotes: Writes semgrep.sarif — the SAST artifact — NOT a parallel opengrep.sarif, and that is the point rather than an oversight. This lane is declared an alias of `sast` (monitor/scanner-checks.mjs CHECK_ALIASES), and an alias means the same helper against the same target writing the same artifact; monitor/test/dark-categories.test.mjs enforces exactly that and rejected the two-file version. The filename is historical, the engine is not lost: SARIF records it in runs[].tool.driver.name, which reads 'Opengrep OSS 1.26.0' when this lane produced the file. Only one of the two ever runs in a group, so there is nothing to clobber. Same failure mode as Semgrep and the same detection: a 404'd ruleset loads ZERO rules and exits 7, `|| true` swallows the exit code, and the SARIF is the only surviving evidence — verified 2026-08-11 that opengrep writes toolExecutionNotifications at level error and that parseReport scores it `noscan` rather than a clean 0. `--pro-intrafile` is Semgrep-Pro-only and is rejected outright ('unknown option'). THE BINARY UNPACKS ITSELF: `opengrep` is a onefile bundle that extracts to ~/.cache/opengrep/<version>/ on first run and re-reads that copy on every later one. Undeclared, the sandbox denied the read, the bundle took the unreadable copy for a missing one, tried to rewrite it and exited 2 with `failed to open '…/opengrep.bin' for writing` — no SARIF on any repo (measured 2026-09-30, cobolwork and ironwork). It is declared a READ, not a write, so a scanned tree that compromises the parser cannot replace the binary the operator runs next; a newly installed version must therefore run once outside the sandbox (`opengrep --version`, which the run path's tool-provenance probe already does) before a scan can use it, and until then the lane exits 2 and reports a void.

checks.description: Deep taint / data-flow SAST (CodeQL). Heavy: builds a database, so it lives in the 'deep' group only.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are fixing deep data-flow / taint findings from CodeQL (codeql.sarif, JavaScript/TypeScript). Unlike a pattern SAST, each CodeQL result traces a path from an untrusted SOURCE to a dangerous SINK — read runs[].results[].codeFlows to see the full flow, not just the flagged line. Fix by breaking the taint path: validate/sanitize at the source, or use a safe sink API (parameterized query, safe DOM API, path canonicalization + allowlist, no shell string interpolation). Prefer a fix at the sink so all sources are covered. Verify the flow is actually reachable before acting; if a result is a proven false positive, suppress it narrowly. Explain the source→sink path for each fix and show the diff.
local: test -r "$CW_ROOT/manifests/codeql-filters.txt" || { echo "sast-codeql: REFUSED to index unbounded — $CW_ROOT/manifests/codeql-filters.txt is missing or unreadable. An unfiltered CodeQL database indexes generated output (reports/, map/data/) and inflated one area to 638 phantom highs. Writing NO sarif, which classifies noscan — a visible void, never a clean zero." >&2; exit 1; }; export LGTM_INDEX_FILTERS="$(sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*#.*$//' -e '/^[[:space:]]*$/d' "$CW_ROOT/manifests/codeql-filters.txt")"; codeql database create "$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql-db" --language=javascript-typescript --source-root=. --overwrite >"$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql.log" 2>&1 && codeql database analyze "$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql-db" --format=sarif-latest --output="$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql.sarif" >>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql.log" 2>&1; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/codeql.sarif.exit"
checks.formatNotes: A SARIF document must have runs[] array (REQUIRED by SARIF spec). Absence of runs[] indicates the tool never ran (error object, stub, or wrong format), not "scanned and found nothing". An empty runs:[] IS valid — distinguishes "we looked" from "we never looked".

checks.description: Go-specific SAST (gosec) — the Go equivalent of the CodeQL lanes, which are javascript-typescript and java only. Semgrep's Go coverage is generic pattern rules; gosec adds taint analysis Semgrep does not carry (G703 path traversal, G705 XSS, G706 log injection) plus Go-idiomatic rules (G115 integer overflow, G301/G302/G306 file modes, G404 weak PRNG). Measured 2026-08-02 on hashicorp/terraform: semgrep 114 findings, gosec 756, and gosec was the only lane to report the TLS, Slowloris and hardcoded-credential classes.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging Go security findings from gosec (gosec.sarif). Read runs[].results[] — ruleId, message.text, and the file+region. Triage by CLASS before fixing anything, because gosec's raw count is dominated by low-value rules: G104 (unhandled errors) is usually hygiene, not a vulnerability, and firing in _test.go or testdata means almost nothing. Prioritise the taint rules (G703 path traversal, G705 XSS, G706 log injection) and the transport/crypto rules (G402 InsecureSkipVerify, G106 InsecureIgnoreHostKey, G501/G505 weak hash imports). For each, establish REACHABILITY first: a finding gated behind an explicit opt-in config field (a `skip_cert_verification` option the operator must set) is a documented choice, not a defect, and a weak-hash import that implements a product's own `md5()`/`sha1()` language function cannot be removed without removing the feature. Fix real findings at the sink: canonicalise + allowlist paths, encode output, derive identity from the authenticated principal. Record every dismissal WITH its reason — an undocumented dismissal is indistinguishable from not looking. Show the diff per fix.
checks.formatNotes: Gosec outputs SARIF; see sast-codeql notes. Additionally: gosec has many low-value rules (G104 unhandled-error in _test.go). Triage by reachability: is the error path reachable, and is it genuinely security-critical? A documented opt-in flag is a choice, not a defect.

checks.description: Python-specific security static analysis (Bandit 1.8.6) — closes a real void: before this lane, Python's only source-level security coverage was CodeQL (plus whatever fraction of Semgrep's generic rules apply, which cwe-map.json already grades ruleset-dependent). Bandit finds Python-shaped vulnerability classes CodeQL's generic ruleset can miss: subprocess/os.system with shell=True, eval/exec on untrusted input, weak hashes (MD5/SHA1), insecure deserialization (pickle.loads, unsafe yaml.load), hardcoded bind-all interfaces, SQL string concatenation. Pure AST parsing, verified against a real install: no compilation, no build step, no execution of the scanned repo's code — clears the untrusted-execution objection standing against lint-rust-clippy (which type-checks and therefore runs build.rs/proc-macros; Bandit does neither). `sev` is derived from Bandit's own issue_severity field ALONE, never issue_confidence — the two are independent axes in Bandit's output, and folding confidence into severity is the GuardDog capability-* defect (a likelihood-of-true-positive signal dressed as impact) recurring in a new tool. Bandit has NO SARIF output format (verified against `bandit --help`, 1.8.6: -f {csv,custom,html,json,screen,txt,xml,yaml}) — this reads its native -f json shape.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging Python security findings from Bandit (bandit.json). Each result carries test_id (e.g. B404, B602), issue_severity (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW — this IS the fleet severity, already mapped) and issue_confidence (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW — how sure Bandit is the pattern is what it looks like, embedded in the message text, NEVER treated as severity: a high-confidence hardcoded-secret in a test fixture matters less than a low-confidence SQL fragment on an authenticated admin path). Work HIGH severity first. subprocess/os.system findings (B602-B605): replace shell=True with an argv list, or validate/allowlist the input if a shell is genuinely required. eval/exec (B307, B102): remove entirely if possible; if not, explain why untrusted input cannot reach it. Weak hash (B303, B324): MD5/SHA1 used for anything security-relevant (not checksums of non-sensitive data) needs SHA-256+ or a KDF for passwords. Insecure deserialization (B301, B506): pickle.loads/yaml.load on untrusted input is remote code execution — use yaml.safe_load or reject pickle entirely for data crossing a trust boundary. Hardcoded bind (B104): 0.0.0.0 in a bind call needs justification or a narrower interface. If a finding is a false positive (a test fixture, a deliberately-scoped internal tool), dismiss it WITH the reason recorded — an undocumented dismissal is indistinguishable from not looking. Show the diff per file.
checks.formatNotes: Bandit's native -f json, NOT SARIF -- verified 2026-09-01 against a real install (1.8.6) that this format does not exist for this tool. {results:[{filename,line_number,test_id,issue_severity,issue_confidence,issue_text,issue_cwe:{id}}], errors:[]}. Exit is non-zero merely for FINDING issues, so ran/did-not-run is judged from whether the JSON parses into this shape, never from the exit code.
checks.notes: Cost class not yet measured on a real corpus repo -- bin/python-lane-scan.mjs's CW_PYTHON_LANE_TIMEOUT_MS default (120s) is a conservative placeholder, not a measured bound. Measure on the 100randomrepos corpus before trusting a tighter timeout.

checks.description: Python correctness and hygiene lint (ruff 0.16.5) — NOT a security scan, kept out of the SAST category deliberately so a linter can never earn a green SAST row, the same rule lint-go-golangci and lint-rust-clippy are held to. Restricted to --select E,F,W,C90 --ignore S: pyflakes-class errors (F, undefined names/unused imports), pycodestyle (E/W), mccabe complexity (C90). Explicitly EXCLUDES ruff's S-prefixed rules (flake8-bandit-equivalent) — those are security-shaped and belong to sast-python-bandit, not here; turning them on here would be the exact naming defect lint-rust-clippy's own notes warn against, in the opposite direction (a lint lane quietly reaching into the security axis). Verified: ruff --output-format sarif is real (ruff check --help, 0.16.5) and is reused as-is.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging Python lint findings from ruff (ruff.sarif). runs[].results[] carry ruleId = the ruff rule code (F401, E501, C901, ...) — correctness and hygiene defects, NOT vulnerabilities. Triage by class: F-codes (pyflakes) are usually real — unused imports and undefined names are close to free to fix and worth doing; E/W-codes (pycodestyle) are mostly cosmetic, fix the ones that are cheap and skip the rest rather than churning the diff; C901 (complexity) findings need a judgement call — split the function only if the complexity is masking a real bug, not for the metric alone. Record every dismissal with its reason.
checks.formatNotes: SARIF 2.1.0, driver `ruff`, ruleId = the ruff rule code. Exit is non-zero merely for FINDING issues, so ran/did-not-run is judged from the parsed output by bin/python-lane-scan.mjs, never from the exit code.
checks.notes: Cost class not yet measured on a real corpus repo -- same placeholder caveat as sast-python-bandit.

checks.description: Go correctness and hygiene lint (golangci-lint 2.13.2) — NOT a security scan, and kept out of the SAST category deliberately so a linter can never earn a green SAST row, the same rule deno-lint and actions-actionlint are held to. gosec already owns Go security; this covers what gosec has no rules for: unchecked errors (errcheck), ineffectual assignments, and the staticcheck SA* classes where real bugs hide. Runs through bin/go-lane-scan.mjs so it walks to every go.mod rather than only the repo root — 13 of 29 Go repos in the 100randomrepos corpus carry their module one or more levels down.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging Go lint findings from golangci-lint (golangci.sarif). runs[].results[] carry ruleId = the LINTER name (errcheck, ineffassign, staticcheck, ...), not a rule number. These are correctness and hygiene defects, NOT vulnerabilities — say so plainly and do not inflate them. Triage by linter: errcheck's unchecked-error findings are usually hygiene and in _test.go are close to noise; ineffassign and the staticcheck SA* checks are where real bugs hide — a value computed and discarded, a nil path, a condition that is always true. Fix what changes behaviour and leave the cosmetic ones rather than churning the diff. Record every dismissal with its reason.
checks.formatNotes: SARIF 2.1.0, driver `golangci-lint`, ruleId = linter name. Exit is non-zero merely for FINDING issues (as gosec's is), so the ran/did-not-run decision is made from the parsed output by bin/go-lane-scan.mjs, never from the status.

checks.description: Go dependency + stdlib vulnerabilities with REACHABILITY (govulncheck). Unlike OSV/grype, which report any advisory touching the module graph, govulncheck returns a call stack when a vulnerable symbol is actually reachable — a module-level trace with no stack means present-but-unreached. Measured 2026-08-02 on hashicorp/terraform: OSV and grype each reported GO-2026-5932 11 times (once per nested go.mod); govulncheck returned it with no call stack and nothing in the tree imports the affected package. Same advisory, three tools, and only this one could say it was unreachable.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are remediating Go vulnerabilities from govulncheck (govulncheck.json, JSON-lines). Each record is either an `osv` (an advisory definition) or a `finding` (this module is affected). READ THE TRACE on every finding: a trace whose entries carry a `function` is a proven call path — fix those first. A trace with only `module`/`version` and no function is module-level, meaning the advisory applies to a module in the graph but govulncheck could NOT prove the vulnerable package is imported; verify by grepping the import path before you touch anything, because these are frequently already mitigated. Fix reachable findings by bumping to the fixed version in go.mod and running `go mod tidy`; for a transitive dependency use a `replace` or bump the intermediate. Note that a Go monorepo can have MANY nested go.mod files — a bump in the root does not fix a nested module, and each must be updated separately. If an advisory has no fixed version (an unmaintained-package advisory), the remedy is migration to the maintained fork, not a version bump. Re-run to confirm the finding cleared.
checks.notes: govulncheck requires a Go toolchain matching or exceeding the repo's `go` directive — an older toolchain cannot load the module graph and the scan fails OPEN. The check declares tool:go so a missing/old toolchain blocks visibly rather than passing empty.
checks.formatNotes: Govulncheck outputs JSON-lines (one osv or finding per line). A finding with trace[] containing function entries is proven reachable; findings with only module/version are potentially unimported. Grep the import path to verify before acting. A missing fixed version requires migration to the maintained fork, not version bumps.

checks.description: Dependency vulnerabilities via OSV-Scanner (Docker; auto-detects npm/maven/gradle/go/...)
checks.remediationPrompt: You are remediating dependency CVEs found by OSV-Scanner (osv.sarif). Each result names a vulnerable package@version and its manifest/lockfile path. For each: identify the smallest safe upgrade to a fixed version, prefer a patch/minor bump, and update BOTH the manifest and the lockfile so the resolved tree actually changes (a manifest-only edit or an unrun `resolutions`/`overrides` leaves the scanned lockfile still vulnerable). Handle transitive vulns via the package manager's override mechanism (npm `overrides`, yarn `resolutions`, Gradle constraints) and re-run install. If no fixed version exists, say so and note mitigation/acceptance. Group fixes by ecosystem, show the manifest+lockfile diff, and re-run the scan to confirm the count dropped.
local: LOCKM=""; LOCKL=""; if [ -n "${CW_LOCKFILE_DIR:-}" ] && [ -d "$CW_LOCKFILE_DIR" ]; then LOCKM="--mount $CW_LOCKFILE_DIR:/locks:ro"; for f in "$CW_LOCKFILE_DIR"/*; do [ -f "$f" ] && LOCKL="$LOCKL -L /locks/$(basename "$f")"; done; fi; SBX=$(node "$CW_ROOT/bin/sandbox.mjs" --posture lookup --name "${CW_CONTAINER_NAME:-cw-cli-repo-deps-osv}-osv" --mount-source "$PWD:/src:ro" $LOCKM) || { echo "sandbox refused to emit flags -- writing NO sarif, which classifies noscan rather than clean" >&2; exit 2; }; docker run $SBX ghcr.io/google/osv-scanner:latest scan source -r --call-analysis=go --experimental-exclude 'g:**/.git/**' --format=sarif $LOCKL /src > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/osv.sarif" 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/osv.log"; rc=$?; echo $rc > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/osv.sarif.exit"; if [ $rc -gt 1 ]; then echo "osv-scanner exited $rc (127=tool error, 128=no packages scanned) -- NOT a clean scan" >> "$CW_REPORT_DIR/osv.log"; fi; if [ $rc -gt 1 ] && [ $rc -ne 128 ]; then exit $rc; fi
checks.notes: Exit codes are load-bearing and `|| true` erased them: osv-scanner returns 0 clean, 1 VULNERABILITIES FOUND, 127 tool error, 128 no packages scanned. The old body collapsed all four to pass, so a tool error and an empty scan both recorded as a clean run -- the same silent-green shape as npm-audit's ENOLOCK husk. Now 0 and 1 pass (severity comes from parsing osv.sarif, not from the exit code) and anything higher fails with the code logged. EXIT 128 IS A VOID, NOT A FAILURE, AND THE WITNESS IS NOW WRITTEN. `exit $rc` on 128 recorded 5 repos as FAILED lanes with an empty reason (RxJava, caffeine, TranslationPlugin, brave, apollo on 127) when what happened was that osv indexed no package sources -- a coverage void whose cause lives in preflight, not in the repo. 128 now falls through with an empty sarif, which classifyReport reads as noscan; the rollup appends preflight's verdict so the reader learns WHICH void (blind vs no-surface). 127 still exits, because a tool error is not a void. And $rc is written to osv.sarif.exit for every outcome: this lane had no second witness at all, so an empty artifact and a crashed tool were the same absence. The image is pulled ONCE PER SWEEP by monitor/images.mjs (see the top-level `images` list), bounded, with presence + digest recorded in batch-manifest.json -- not `--pull=always` per repo. The freshness argument is unchanged: `:latest` is NOT self-updating, `docker run` reuses the cached image indefinitely, and a stale scanner silently misses every advisory published since it was pulled (measured 2026-08-04: 6 weeks old). The per-repo placement was the defect: 100 registry round-trips a batch, and on sweep-20260822153004 one stalled pull held the first repo for 8.9 h with no alarm. An unreachable registry still must not read as clean: the preamble records {pulled:false, reason} and the batch carries it; a CLI `commitwork run` outside a sweep does no pull and runs the cached tag, which tool-version-deps-osv.json records. --experimental-exclude 'g:**/.git/**' (2026-08-11) because bin/gate-tests.mjs materialises pristine HEAD worktrees at .git/gate-head-<pid> and a scan racing a live gate (or meeting a leaked tree) indexed their lockfiles as this repo's: 124 phantom issues, every one a package-lock.json inside a transient checkout that no longer exists -- the measuring apparatus scanning the OTHER measuring apparatus's leavings (same class as the zizmor 1753-findings incident). PATTERN FORM MATTERS AND WAS PROBED, not assumed: the documented bare-dirname form (`--experimental-exclude .git`) does NOT exclude it (planted lockfile still scanned -- an exclusion that does not exclude reads as coverage), `g:.git/**` also fails; `g:**/.git/**` and `r:/\.git/` both verified excluding the planted .git lockfile while the real tree stays scanned. .git/ is never source; nothing legitimate is lost. call analysis: --call-analysis=go is ENABLED (verified 2026-08-20 to add no network endpoint beyond api.osv.dev, which this lane already contacts; Go call analysis does not run build scripts — that caveat attaches to rust). Its experimental_analysis.called field is NEVER used to suppress a finding:  is emitted even when call analysis was not requested at all, so it means "not determined to be called", not "unreachable". Only called:true carries information. UNPINNED-FETCH EXEMPTION (2026-08-20): `bin/test/no-unpinned-fetch.test.mjs` fails any scan-time command that fetches an unpinned artifact, and this line is the ONE deliberate exception in the roster -- `:latest` plus a per-sweep pull is an unpinned pull by construction, and that is the point, for the reason two paragraphs up: the image IS the advisory database, so a digest pin freezes the database and a frozen vulnerability database reports 'clean' about advisories it has never heard of. The exemption is written down in the gate itself, keyed to this check id and this file, with this reason -- it is not a pattern hole that any future `:latest` can slip through, and if this command is ever edited to fetch something else the exemption no longer matches and the gate bites. Contrast supply-chain-guarddog below, which IS pinned and says why the trade lands the other way.
checks.formatNotes: OSV-Scanner outputs SARIF in Docker. Check that both manifest and lockfile are updated together — a manifest-only edit leaves the scanned lockfile vulnerable. Handle transitive vulns via npm overrides / yarn resolutions / Gradle constraints, not lockfile edits. osv-declared.json is written beside osv.sarif by bin/osv-declared.mjs and records, per manifest, whether the repository STATES each reported package@version. It is captured HERE, at scan time, rather than derived in the rollup: rollup.mjs can reach the repo, but reading the working tree there would make a re-roll's answer depend on the tree as it is now rather than as it was when the batch was scanned, and corrected-history is only worth anything if a re-roll reads nothing but the batch. `|| true` because an absent verdict file must leave today's behaviour intact — the rollup applies no demotion without it. EGRESS: registry. osv-scanner queries api.osv.dev for every package it parses. This is a container lane (posture lookup): the container posture is the isolation, and the host wrapper is not applied.

checks.description: OWASP dep-scan over the dependency graph, in a container with the network severed. A SECOND OPINION on the CVE lane rather than an extension of it: same advisory data, independent engine, plus the only reachability ADJUDICATION available outside Go.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging OWASP dep-scan output (depscan.json is the summary; the CycloneDX VDR named in `detail` carries the rows). Read `reachability.state` FIRST. If it is `not-produced` the analyser wrote no slices — usually a tree with no installed dependencies — and you have NO reachability information: do not describe anything as unreachable, say the analysis did not run and why. Where state is `analysed`, work the findings dep-scan marked `exploitable` first: those are the ones it traced a path to. Everything else is `unadjudicated`, which means not assessed, NOT safe. Cross-check each finding against the osv lane for the same repo — agreement raises confidence, and a disagreement (dep-scan adjudicating a path osv does not carry, or osv reporting a package dep-scan’s graph does not contain) is the most valuable row on the page and should be reported as a disagreement rather than silently resolved. Recommend version bumps by package, and never claim a fix reduces risk you did not measure.
checks.notes: SANDBOX IS THE PRECONDITION, NOT A HARDENING EXTRA. Resolving dependencies executes the scanned repo’s build logic (gradle evaluates build.gradle, pip runs setup.py on an sdist, cdxgen shells out to the tree’s package manager), and this fleet scans arbitrary third-party repositories. bin/depscan-scan.sh therefore REFUSES to run on the host: no docker, no scan. It uses two containers so that no single one holds both the source and the network — warm pulls the VDB with network on and nothing mounted, scan mounts the source read-only under --network none, plus --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, uid 1000, pids/memory limits and a tmpfs /tmp. That isolation COSTS coverage (an offline analyser cannot install what it needs to slice), which is why `coverage` and `reachability.state` travel in every report and why CW_DEPSCAN_ALLOW_NET=1 exists to make the opposite trade explicitly rather than by drift. EXCLUDED FROM THE SEVERITY SUM (monitor/extractors.mjs TOTALS_EXCLUDE) for maliciousPackages’ reason: parseOsv already counted this advisory data, so summing would double-count one dependency graph. OPERATIONAL: the default vulnerability database is 57.3 GB on disk and is NOT sparse — evaluate --vdb-time/--vdb-scope before running this fleet-wide.
checks.formatNotes: depscan.json is a SUMMARY written by bin/depscan-scan.sh, not dep-scan’s own output; the CycloneDX VDR and SBOMs land in depscan-raw/ and are named in `detail`. ran:false is a VOID, never a clean tree. THE TRAP THIS FORMAT EXISTS TO DOCUMENT: dep-scan’s analysis.state is `in_triage` by DEFAULT — it means not adjudicated, not reachable. Measured on vercel/satori 2026-08-22: 105 findings, 100 in_triage, and universal-usages.slices.json empty, i.e. ZERO adjudications from an analyser that never ran. Only `exploitable` is a proof; a run whose slicer produced nothing carries reachability.state:not-produced and NO reachability counts, because 0-reachable and no-answer are different claims. Verified against the ghcr.io/owasp-dep-scan/dep-scan image on 2026-08-22 (105 vulns, 1140 components, network severed, exit 0).

checks.description: JVM dependency CVEs via Trivy `fs` — reads project manifests (pom.xml, gradle.lockfile) AND still recurses into a built Spring Boot fat jar's BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar. Was `rootfs` until 2026-08-21; see formatNotes for why that mattered.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are remediating JVM dependency CVEs found by Trivy (trivy-jvm.json). Read Results[].Vulnerabilities[] — each has PkgName, InstalledVersion, FixedVersion, Severity, and VulnerabilityID. These are the jars actually bundled in the built artifact, so the fix must land in the build definition. For each vuln with a FixedVersion: bump it in build.gradle / pom.xml. For a TRANSITIVE dependency, pin it with a Gradle constraint inside `dependencyManagement { dependencies { dependency ... } }` (a bare `constraints{}` block loses to Spring's dependency-management plugin) or a Maven `<dependencyManagement>` entry — then REBUILD so BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar changes and re-scan. Work CRITICAL/HIGH first. If a bump is gated (breaking major), state the reachability risk and the accepted-medium rationale. Show the build-file diff.
local: trivy fs --scanners vuln --skip-dirs reference,reports --quiet --format json --output "$CW_REPORT_DIR/trivy-jvm.json" . 2>"$CW_REPORT_DIR/trivy-jvm.log"; echo $? > "$CW_REPORT_DIR/trivy-jvm.json.exit"
checks.formatNotes: MODE MATTERS, and it was wrong until 2026-08-21. `trivy rootfs` scans an UNPACKED CONTAINER FILESYSTEM — installed packages and built jars — while `trivy fs` scans a PROJECT DIRECTORY and reads its manifests. Pointed at a source tree, rootfs reads the declared dependencies of nothing. Measured on apolloconfig_apollo at one commit: rootfs = 2 packages / 0 vulns, fs = 1255 packages / 527 vulns; the fleet-wide rescan that followed surfaced 5,709 findings the first pass had reported as absent. `fs` still walks built jars, so the fat-jar case is not lost by the change. STILL BLIND TO GRADLE WITHOUT A LOCKFILE: neither mode resolves build.gradle or gradle/libs.versions.toml, so a Gradle project committing no gradle.lockfile catalogues ZERO packages and — until an empty catalogue reports noscan — returns `pass`, indistinguishable from a genuine zero. Eight repos in 100randomrepos sit in exactly that state (RxJava, TranslationPlugin, calcite, caffeine, fresco, grpc-java, junit-framework, slint). Fixes must land in build.gradle / pom.xml, and for the fat-jar path the artifact must be REBUILT so the jar actually changes. Transitive deps use Gradle constraints or Maven dependencyManagement. EGRESS: registry. trivy fetches its vulnerability database from ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db into ~/Library/Caches/trivy (~/.cache/trivy on Linux); the scan itself reads the tree. Under the host sandbox the filesystem is confined and the network is open (isolation fs-only).

checks.description: Dependency CVEs for Gradle projects with NO lockfile, via declared coordinates + deps.dev transitive closure + OSV. A FLOOR, not a ceiling — Gradle constraints/resolutionStrategy/BOMs/plugins can override a declared version invisibly.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are fixing dependency vulnerabilities found by resolving this Gradle project's DECLARED coordinates (gradle/libs.versions.toml, build.gradle literals, buildSrc constants) through deps.dev, then querying OSV. READ THE CAVEAT BEFORE ACTING ON ANY FINDING. This is a declared-version resolution, so it is a FLOOR on the real exposure, never a ceiling. The build may pin a different version through constraints, resolutionStrategy, a platform BOM or a plugin, and it may pull dependencies this lane never saw. Confirm the version Gradle actually resolves before changing anything — run the dependency report yourself if you own the build. Do NOT run it as part of a scan: executing a third-party build is the untrusted-code execution this fleet exists to detect, which is the whole reason this lane resolves through a published graph instead. Fix by raising the declared version in the version catalog or build file. For a TRANSITIVE finding prefer a constraint or a BOM bump over pinning the transitive directly, so the fix survives the next upgrade of its parent rather than silently reverting. Every result states whether it is direct or transitive — say which you are fixing and why, and if a finding cannot be reached from any declared dependency, say that instead of raising a version to make a number go down.
checks.formatNotes: NETWORK-DEPENDENT, and that is the shape of its failure: deps.dev and OSV are both remote, so an offline run must degrade to NOSCAN and never to zero. The tool enforces that itself — it deletes its report and exits non-zero when deps.dev resolves nothing or no OSV batch succeeds, so an unreachable network cannot be read as a clean project. It also refuses when no coordinate is resolvable at all (a repo declaring everything through a BOM), rather than reporting an empty scan. Emits SARIF deliberately so monitor/sarif-read.mjs owns the did-it-run decision — nine hand-rolled readers were just consolidated there, and a bespoke format would reopen exactly what that consolidation closed. The floor caveat rides on the run invocation AND in every result message, so nothing downstream can keep the count while dropping the qualification.

checks.description: Gradle wrapper integrity — where ./gradlew fetches its Gradle distribution from, and what the committed gradle-wrapper.jar and gradlew script are. Static: runs no Gradle, needs no container.
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging Gradle wrapper integrity findings (gradle-wrapper.json). READ THE SCOPE FIRST: this lane checks the wrapper FETCH PATH only. It does not cover build.gradle configuration-time code, gradle.properties jvmargs (-javaagent: is code execution), settings.gradle pluginManagement repositories, or wrappers in sub-modules — a zero here says nothing about any of those. For distribution-url-off-vendor: establish whether the host is a legitimate corporate mirror before doing anything else; if it is not, treat the repository as hostile and do not run ./gradlew. For distribution-url-plaintext: the toolchain is fetched over a channel any network position can rewrite — pin https and add distributionSha256Sum. For distribution-checksum-undeclared: add distributionSha256Sum so Gradle itself detects a substituted download. For wrapper-jar-oversized or gradlew-oversized: do not open the file to look; the genuine artifacts are ~50 KB and a few hundred lines. Never recommend running ./gradlew to reproduce a finding.
checks.notes: WHY THIS EXISTS SEPARATELY FROM deps-gradle-declared. That lane resolves declared coordinates through deps.dev without executing Gradle, and is the right default. This one covers what happens BEFORE any build file is read: ./gradlew fetches a Gradle distribution from a URL the SCANNED REPOSITORY chooses, and executes gradle-wrapper.jar, a committed binary nobody diffs. Both are checkable statically and neither was checked. THE JAR AND SCRIPT HASHES ARE PUBLISHED FOR CROSS-REPO COMPARISON: both are GENERATED by Gradle rather than authored by the project, so two repos declaring one version should agree, and disagreement is the only shape a substitution can take. Measured on 100randomrepos 2026-08-22: 7 wrapper repos, 6 declared versions, ONE comparable and FIVE unexaminable because only one repo declares them — which is also the cheapest way to defeat the cross-check, so `unexaminable` is counted rather than left as silence. A jar is never asserted GOOD without a reference list; CW_GRADLE_CHECKSUMS supplies one when it exists and its absence reports as no-reference-list.
checks.formatNotes: gradle-wrapper.json carries {ran, applicable, findings[], scope, doesNotCover, declaredVersion, jarSha256, gradlewSha256, checksumCheck}. applicable:false is a repo with NO wrapper — nothing to scan, not a void, and the extractor reads it as nosrc. ran:false is a genuine void. THE SCOPE FIELD IS PART OF THE RESULT: scope is "wrapper-fetch-path" and doesNotCover names what is outside it, because a zero from this lane would otherwise read as covering build.gradle, which it emphatically does not. checksumCheck:no-reference-list means the jar hash was computed and compared to NOTHING — unknown, never good. An unreadable properties file yields ONE finding and nothing derived from it: the first cut emitted four, two of them assertions about a file nobody read. Verified against 7 real Gradle repos on 2026-08-22.

checks.description: Known-vulnerable JS library detection (retire.js) by FILE CONTENT, not by manifest — the lane that sees a library the lockfile never declares (a bundled copy inside another package's dist, or a vendored asset with no package entry at all).
checks.notes: THE GATE WAS THE BUG. This check has always run `retire --path .`, which is a content-signature scan and needs no package manifest — but it was gated `appliesIfExists: [package.json]`, so the one class of target it uniquely covers, a tree with vulnerable JS and no manifest, was the one class it never ran on. Gated on JS source extensions instead, matching sast-codeql, so the gate now matches what the command actually does. Why it earns its own lane rather than folding into deps-osv/npm-audit: measured 2026-08-01 on a client admin console, retire found quill 1.3.7 inside react-quill/dist/react-quill.js and vue 2.6.14 inside a chart.js docs asset — two libraries no lockfile names, invisible to every manifest-gated lane. KNOWN LIMIT: retire's database is curated, so a clean result is not proof of safety. Verified 2026-08-02 that it returns zero entries for sitemap/vendor/three.min.js (607KB, ~4 years old, publicly served), which stays an open coverage hole rather than being credited to this check. PINNED 2026-08-20 to retire@5.4.3 (registry latest that day). It was a bare `npx --yes retire`, i.e. a supply-chain fetch of whatever the registry served at scan time, INSIDE the supply-chain scanner -- the one place a compromised or merely changed publish must not be able to walk in unannounced. retire's vulnerability data ships inside the package, so the pin does freeze that data: bumping this version is a real maintenance obligation, not cosmetic, and it is deliberately a visible literal so `bin/test/no-unpinned-fetch.test.mjs` can see it and renovate/an operator can find it by grep.

checks.description: Supply-chain / malicious-package detection (Socket) — typosquats, install-script malware, obfuscation that CVE scanners cannot see
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging supply-chain alerts from Socket (socket.json) — these are NOT CVEs but package-BEHAVIOUR risks: install/postinstall scripts, network/filesystem/shell access at install time, obfuscated code, typosquats, protestware, newly-published or unmaintained packages. For each alert read the package name, version, and issue type. Treat a typosquat or install-script-malware alert as an incident: confirm you meant to install that exact package (check for a one-character-off name against the popular package), and if malicious, remove it, purge it from the lockfile, and rotate any credential the machine that ran install had access to. For high-risk-but-legitimate packages (a real build tool with an install script), document why it is trusted. Prefer a maintained alternative for abandoned packages. Show the dependency diff and an incident note for anything confirmed malicious.
checks.notes: NOT in `all`, and that is a quota decision rather than a coverage one. Socket's free tier is 1,000 scans/month; this fleet has 23 repos carrying a package.json, so a nightly `all` sweep costs 690/month against that ceiling — it fits, but with 31% headroom and no alarm when it runs out. An exhausted quota returns an API refusal, and a refusal lands in socket.json looking exactly like the {ok:false} husk that _countArray still credits as `ran` — so running out would restore the false green this lane was cured of, with a real credential behind it. Run it deliberately: `node monitor/sweep.mjs supply-chain <area>`.
checks.formatNotes: Socket outputs JSON with issues array. Keys: package name/version, issue type (install-scripts, obfuscated, new-releases, etc.). Each issue carries a reason — a typosquat or install-script-malware must be treated as incident (confirm exact package name, check for name typos, rotate creds if installed). `npm_config_registry` is set because the CLI's startup self-update check otherwise reads the nearest .npmrc for a registry URL, finds ~/.npmrc by walking up from the tree, and dies at EPERM on it: the sandbox withholds that file because it holds npm tokens. Measured 2026-09-30 on cobolwork: `Fatal error: EPERM … open '~/.npmrc'`, exit 1, nothing scanned. With the variable set that read never happens.

checks.description: Package-metadata heuristics across the resolved npm tree (GuardDog, Apache-2.0) — typosquats, deceptive authors, compromised/unclaimed maintainer email domains, risky-new/direct-URL deps, bundled binaries
checks.remediationPrompt: You are triaging GuardDog findings (guarddog.sarif). These are HEURISTIC registry-metadata signals over the resolved npm tree, not confirmed malware and not CVEs — the OSV MAL- lane (osv.sarif) carries confirmed-malicious packages, and a GuardDog hit is a prompt to look, not a verdict. Read each rule id: `typosquatting` means the name is one edit away from a popular package (confirm you meant this exact package before anything else, and if you did not, treat it as an incident — remove it, purge the lockfile, rotate any credential the install machine could reach); `deceptive_author`, `potentially_compromised_email_domain` and `unclaimed_maintainer_email_domain` mean the publishing identity is weak or hijackable (check whether the package changed hands recently); `risky_new_dependency` means it is newly published (pin it and re-review); `direct_url_dependency` and `bundled_binary` mean code enters the tree outside the registry's integrity guarantees (justify it in writing or replace it). MOST OF WHAT YOU WILL SEE IS THE OTHER RULE FAMILY, and it is not registry metadata at all: `capability-*` and `threat-*` rules are source analysis over the published tarball and their message names the file and line inside it ("On package: X version: Y - Detects ... in file package/dist/index.js:38"). Measured on the first real run, 16 of 16 findings were this family. Triage them by asking whether the capability is EXPLAINED BY WHAT THE PACKAGE IS FOR: `capability-network-outbound` in an HTTP client or a docs site bundler is its job; the same rule in a date formatter or a colour library is not. `capability-process-spawn` is normal in build tooling and a red flag in a runtime dependency. `threat-runtime-environment-read` is worth a look wherever it appears because that is how credentials leave a machine, but it is also how every library reads NODE_ENV - check WHICH variables. `threat-runtime-obfuscation-*` on a MINIFIED bundle is expected and near-worthless as a signal; the same rule on unminified source is the real thing. Do not open one finding per capability across a dependency tree - group by package, decide once whether that package is trusted for what it does, and record that. Expect false positives on legitimate scoped/internal packages — for each one you dismiss, record WHY, because an undocumented dismissal is indistinguishable from not looking. Show the dependency diff for anything you change.
checks.notes: MUST be pointed at package.json, NOT package-lock.json. GuardDog's parse_requirements (npm_project_scanner.py) reads the top-level `dependencies` map expecting name -> version STRING, which is package.json's shape. Against a lockfile it fails two ways and neither says so: lockfileVersion 2 has those keys with OBJECT values, so resolve_npm_alias() raises `TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object` and the run dies mid-scan; lockfileVersion 3 has no top-level `dependencies` at all, so it parses ZERO packages, exits 0, and writes a rules-only SARIF that reads as a clean tree. Measured 2026-08-10 across the fleet's whole history: 185 runs, 0 findings ever, 158 of them the silent v3 shape and 27 the v2 crash — and the correlation with lockfileVersion is exact. Proven on an internal project, same repo, one path changed: /src/package-lock.json scanned nothing; /src/package.json returned 22 risks at 10.0/10. The previous note explained the empty results as `verify` being metadata-only rather than per-package source analysis. THAT EXPLANATION IS ALSO FALSE, measured 2026-08-10 on the first repo to produce real output: `verify` emits `capability-*` and `threat-*` rules whose messages name a file and line INSIDE the dependency tarball ("On package: redocusaurus version: 2.5.2 - Detects network request capabilities in file package/dist/index.js:38"). That is per-package source analysis, under `verify`. The driver declares 62 rules spanning BOTH families: registry-metadata (typosquatting, deceptive_author, risky_new_dependency, direct_url_dependency, bundled_binary, metadata_mismatch) and source-derived capability/threat rules, and on a real repo it was the capability/threat family that fired, 16 of 16. The metadata-only claim survived a rewrite of this very note - it was kept as 'real and still worth knowing' while the bug it had concealed was being fixed. A false explanation is not disarmed by correcting the thing it was hiding. Docker rather than the pipx CLI so no Python toolchain is required — same pattern as deps-osv. PINNED 2026-08-20 to ghcr.io/datadog/guarddog:v3.2.0 (registry latest that day; the reference was previously UNTAGGED, i.e. implicitly `:latest`, which is the worst of both worlds — unpinned at first pull and then frozen forever at whatever that pull happened to be, silently, with no way to say which build produced a result). And it takes the OPPOSITE decision from deps-osv one entry above deliberately, so the divergence is not read as an oversight: osv-scanner's detection payload IS the advisory database baked into the image, so a pin is a stale database and a per-sweep pull (monitor/images.mjs) is the correct trade. GuardDog's payload is a rule set applied to npm registry metadata and tarballs fetched LIVE at scan time, so the image is the tool and not the data — pinning it costs no freshness in the signal and buys reproducibility for the behaviour this note records (62 rules, two families, the capability/threat family firing 16 of 16 on a real repo). Bumping the tag is a deliberate act and should be accompanied by re-measuring the claims above. `bin/test/no-unpinned-fetch.test.mjs` enforces the pin. DEV DEPENDENCIES ARE OPT-IN, AND NOT PASSING THE FLAG SCANS NOTHING IN A DEVDEPS-ONLY REPO. Measured 2026-09-18 against the pinned v3.2.0 image, two scratch manifests differing only in which map holds shelljs@0.8.5: under `dependencies` 15 capability-* results; under `devDependencies` 0 results, exit 0, all 63 rules loaded — the lane's own false-clean shape; with `--include-dev-dependencies`, 5 results. `guarddog npm verify --help` documents the flag (also settable as GUARDDOG_NPM_INCLUDE_DEV_DEPENDENCIES=true) and states that by default only production dependencies under `dependencies` are scanned. This lane passes it. commitwork itself declares 0 dependencies and 1 devDependency and had therefore scanned clean over an empty package set; an earlier version of this note asserted parse_requirements read both maps, which was never measured and is wrong.

For `kind: shellcheck`, apply the shell fix in the run block (quote expansions, `cd ... || exit`). Do not add `# actionlint-ignore` to silence a finding you have not understood. checks.description: Shell script correctness and injection lint (shellcheck). Preserve behaviour exactly; a quoting fix must not change how many arguments a command receives.
